title: Where Is the Tree? A Rectangle Puzzle | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: Rectangle yard (bank SVG geometry, scaled up: A bottom-left, B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left, AB = 16 along the bottom, BC = 8 on the right). A small green tree icon slides along AB (step through whole-number spots only, don't land on 10 visibly labeled), with two strings from it to A and to C stretching. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: A tree stands on the edge of a yard, exactly as far from one corner as from another.
Where is it? A right triangle is hiding in the yard, and it tells us.
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's find that tree.

scenes.visual: Question text left, figure right with labels A, B, C, D, E, '16' on a dimension line under AB and '8' beside BC (48px+). Line 4: segments EA and EC glow, both marked with matching ticks. Line 5: '? m' label above EA. Line 6: chips 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.
lines: Here's the question.
A rectangular yard A B C D has A B equal to sixteen meters, and B C equal to eight meters.
A tree at point E on side A B
is the same distance from A as from C.
How far is the tree from A, in meters?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: E on the bottom side; EA and EC with matching ticks. Line 2: E C drawn as a dashed slanted line; triangle EBC shaded with a right-angle mark at B. Line 3: 'EA = ?'.
lines: So what do we know? The distance from E to A equals the distance from E to C.
E A runs along the bottom. E C is slanted, and it makes a right triangle with the corner B.
We want E A.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; figure visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Figure left, a table right with columns 'EA', 'EB = 16 − EA', 'EB² + 8²', 'EA²'. Line 2: right triangle EBC highlighted, legs EB and 8, slanted side EC; text 'EB² + 8² = EC²'. Line 3: 'EC = EA, so EB² + 8² must equal EA²'. Line 4: E placed at 6 from A: row '6 | 10 | 164 | 36' red.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: test each choice with the Pythagorean theorem.
Triangle E B C has a right angle at B. So E B squared plus eight squared equals E C squared.
And E C must equal E A. So E B squared plus sixty-four must equal E A squared.
Try six. Then E B is ten, and ten squared plus sixty-four is one hundred sixty-four.
But six squared is just thirty-six.

scenes.visual: E steps to each choice spot (dot to dot, no smooth tween). Line 1: row '8 | 8 | 128 | 64' red. Line 2: row '10 | 6 | 100 | 100' green; triangle EBC labeled 6, 8, 10. Line 3: '6-8-10 triangle', EC = 10 = EA. Line 4: answer badge '10 m' with chime at end of line, choice C highlighted. (Rows 12 and 14 come in the traps scene.)
lines: Try eight. Then E B is eight, and eight squared plus sixty-four is one hundred twenty-eight.
Eight squared is only sixty-four.
Try ten. Then E B is six. Six squared plus sixty-four is one hundred.
And ten squared is one hundred. A match!
Triangle E B C has sides six, eight and ten, so E C is ten, just like E A.
The tree is ten meters from A. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Equation rows on the right, one per line, figure on the left with EA = x, EB = 16 − x, EC = x labeled. Line 2: '(16 − x)² + 8² = x²'. Line 3: '(16 − x)² = 256 − 32x + x²'. Line 4: '256 − 32x + x² + 64 = x²' with the two x² terms fading (cancel). Line 5: '320 = 32x', then 'x = 10'. Line 6: small card.
lines: Here's a way that works even without choices. Call the distance x.
Then E C is also x, and E B is sixteen minus x.
The right triangle says sixteen minus x, squared, plus eight squared, equals x squared.
Sixteen minus x, times sixteen minus x, is two hundred fifty-six, minus sixteen x, minus sixteen x, plus x squared.
Sixteen minus x, squared, opens up to two hundred fifty-six, minus thirty-two x, plus x squared.
Add sixty-four. Now there's an x squared on both sides, so they cancel out.
That leaves three hundred twenty equals thirty-two x. So x is ten. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? When there are no choices to test, or the numbers aren't nice.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red. Line 2: EB = 6 highlighted on the figure. Line 3: BC = 8 highlighted. Line 4: table rows '12 | 4 | 80 | 144' and '14 | 2 | 68 | 196' red. Line 5: 10 chip green.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice A, six, is a real length: it's E B, from the tree to B. But we want the distance from A.
Choice B, eight, is the short side B C. And we just saw eight fails the test.
Choices D and E, twelve and fourteen: the length E B is only four, then two, and the numbers don't match.
Eighty versus one hundred forty-four, and sixty-eight versus one hundred ninety-six.
So here's a great habit. When two distances are equal, write one of them a second way, with a right triangle.

scenes.visual: New rectangle: AB = 18 bottom, BC = 12 right; E on AB with EA = EC ticks.
lines: Ready for a challenge? A bigger yard has A B equal to eighteen meters and B C equal to twelve meters.
A tree at E on side A B is the same distance from A as from C. How far is it from A?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant figure visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: '(18 − x)² + 12² = x²'; '324 − 36x + x² + 144 = x²'; '468 = 36x', 'x = 13' answer badge with chime at end of line 3; check triangle labeled 5, 12, 13.
lines: Let's call it x again. E B is eighteen minus x, and B C is twelve.
Eighteen minus x, times eighteen minus x, is three hundred twenty-four, minus eighteen x, twice, plus x squared.
Eighteen minus x, squared, is three hundred twenty-four, minus thirty-six x, plus x squared.
Add one hundred forty-four, and the x squared terms cancel.
That leaves four hundred sixty-eight equals thirty-six x. So x is thirteen!
Check: E B is five, and a five, twelve, thirteen triangle is a right triangle. It works!
If you got thirteen meters, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: rectangle with the right triangle shaded, text of the rule.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Name the unknown distance. Then write the same distance a second way, with the Pythagorean theorem.
Set the two equal, and solve.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
